body.p: A fixed-capacity string stores up to N characters in N bytes of data memory. It needs no heap and can be used on every target.
body.codeblock: VAR STRING[16] name = "text" VAR STRING[8] tag
body.p: The bracketed value is the capacity in bytes and must be a constant expression. A shorter initializer or assignment is zero-filled up to the full capacity, so the first example's name holds "text" followed by twelve zero bytes; the characters can be inspected with the ordinary subscript syntax.
body.codeblock: VAR STRING[16] name = "abc" VAR BYTE first = name[0] -- 'a' VAR BYTE after = name[3] -- 0
body.p: COUNT on a fixed-capacity string is the declared capacity, not the current text length: COUNT(name) is 16 above, whatever the contents. Use the length returned by the library, or the dynamic string type described in , when the length must vary at run time.

A value that is too long behaves differently for the two write forms. Assigning a string that does not fit copies as much as fits and sets _string_error to string_error_overflow. A concatenation whose result does not fit leaves the destination unchanged and sets _string_error to string_error_overflow. The error byte is described in .

Fixed-capacity strings may be passed to procedures and functions with matching capacity, and string literals are accepted as actuals for such formals: the literal is staged into a compiler string cell, zero-padded to the capacity, and any length up to the capacity compiles. A longer literal is a compile-time error that names the two lengths.
body.codeblock:
PROCEDURE send(STRING[16] IN s) IS ... END PROCEDURE
send("hello") -- staged, zero-padded send("0123456789ABCDEF") -- exactly 16 characters
body.note: Fixed-capacity strings are not heap objects, so they never allocate or fail for lack of heap space. A too-long value is reported through _string_error as described above.
